articles.summary: The European Central Bank raised interest rates. Will the Fed follow? A quarter-point increase in baseline borrowing costs across the bloc came as officials warned of “upside” inflation risks and oil prices shot above $100 a barrel. Fed-funds traders are putting 64% odds that the Fed will do the same next week (arbitrage alert: the chances on Kalshi are a bit lower ). But the ECB’s only job is to manage inflation, while the Fed has a trickier dual task of managing both prices and employment, and so is keeping an eye on a labor market stuck in a “low hire, low fire” defensive equilibrium. Global central banks would prefer to move their interest rates together to avoid warping investment flows and currency markets. (Back in 1986, a Fed compromise was struck to let Germany and Japan cut first.) The post-Covid responses to inflation and, now, slower growth have upset that lockstep instinct as central banks tend to their own economies. — Liz Hoffman

In a matter of moments, thousands of people were incinerated against a bright blue sky. Passengers on a commercial flight became heroes, phoning hasty goodbyes to their loved ones before making an awesome sacrifice. And while monuments to the nation’s security and prosperity were reduced to rubble on television screens, Americans wondered, “Where will the next attack occur?” Answering that question has been a singular preoccupation of federal law enforcement and intelligence agencies since the attacks. It has required legal and institutional reforms, moral clarity, political courage and, above all, a clear-eyed vision of the nature of the threat. The September 11 attacks were not merely criminal acts; they were acts of war, whose terms, targets, and rules of engagement were dictated not by the Geneva Conventions but by jihadists dedicated to the destruction of Western civilization. articles.summary: My new essay in Civitas Outlook tries to trace modern-day constitutional law to that fateful day twenty-five years ago. Every generation has a defining moment. For my generation, it was September 11, 2001. But a quarter century later, more than 30 percent of Americans have no living memory of 9/11 . The conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq have wound down, Guantanamo Bay is mostly closed, and Ground Zero is a museum. Young law students , in particular, might even think that this historical event has no meaningful impact on the law today. Not quite. Indeed, but for September 11, 2001, and the events that followed, constitutional law likely would be unrecognizable today. articles.summary: L ike most Americans, I spent September 11, 2001, filled with both rage and dread. I wanted the United States to find and kill whoever had planned this attack on my country. I knew little about al-Qaeda, but whoever did this, I thought, must pay. As the shock of that day wore off, I began to wonder, as so many others did in America and around the world, Now what? Saying this even 25 years later seems uncharitable, but after the attacks of 9/11, many Americans, and their government, panicked. Worse, the United States institutionalized this panic in the form of new priorities, new programs, and new agencies, so that even when the fear subsided, the intemperate policies driven by that fear remained. Over the next quarter century, America would spend trillions of dollars, pass draconian laws, create a behemoth of a new Cabinet department, militarize law enforcement, and embark on two major military campaigns.
